lesson.title: Where One Message Ends and the Next Begins: Framing
lesson.summary: Framing is how the data link layer marks the boundaries of individual frames within the raw, undifferentiated bit stream the physical layer delivers, using length counts or reserved sentinel patterns to tell receivers where each message starts and stops.
lesson.body:
The physical layer only knows how to send and receive a raw stream of bits, it has no concept of where one message stops and another starts. The data link layer solves this by wrapping data into frames, and the process of marking those boundaries within a continuous bit stream is called framing. Without framing, a receiver looking at an unbroken sequence of 1s and 0s would have no way to know which group of bits belongs to which frame, or even where a frame begins at all.

There are a few standard ways to mark frame boundaries. The simplest is a length count placed at the start of the frame, telling the receiver exactly how many bytes or bits follow. The drawback is that if that length field itself gets corrupted in transit, the receiver loses synchronization for every frame that follows, since it no longer knows where the current frame actually ends. A more robust family of approaches uses special sentinel patterns to mark the start and end of a frame directly, at the cost of needing a way to prevent that same pattern from accidentally appearing inside the data itself, exactly the problem that bit stuffing and byte stuffing, covered next, are built to solve.

Ethernet offers a concrete, real example of framing at work. Every Ethernet frame begins with a 7 byte preamble, an alternating pattern of 1s and 0s, followed by a single Start Frame Delimiter byte with the pattern 10101011. The preamble lets the receiver's clock synchronize with the incoming signal's timing, and the Start Frame Delimiter's distinct final bits tell the receiver exactly where the preamble ends and the real frame, starting with the destination address, begins. Only after recognizing that delimiter does the receiver start counting bits as part of the actual frame contents.

Framing sits squarely at the data link layer for a reason: the physical layer's job ends at delivering a raw signal representing a bit stream, but everything above that, addressing, error detection, and handing data up to the network layer, depends on first knowing where each discrete frame lives within that stream. A corrupted or misidentified frame boundary can cascade into every frame after it being misread, which is why framing schemes are designed to resynchronize quickly after an error rather than simply hoping errors never happen.

Getting the boundaries right is only half the problem, though. Real data is arbitrary, it can, by pure coincidence, contain the exact same bit pattern a protocol reserves as its frame delimiter. If that happens and nothing is done about it, a receiver would mistake ordinary payload data for the start or end of a frame. The two techniques covered next, bit stuffing and byte stuffing, exist specifically to prevent that kind of false alarm without ever changing the actual data being delivered.
